title: Fatty Acid Oxidation Pathways
objectives: Understand the four oxidation pathways for fatty acids
Explain the carnitine shuttle system for mitochondrial import
Describe the enzymatic steps of β-oxidation
Compare mitochondrial and peroxisomal oxidation systems

pathways.title: Oxidation Systems
pathways.content:
Fatty Acid Oxidation Pathways

1. Mitochondrial β-Oxidation

Substrates: LCFAs (C12-C20)

Products: Acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH2

Key Feature: Main energy-generating pathway

2. Peroxisomal β-Oxidation

Substrates: VLCFAs (≥C22)

Products: Shortened FAs for mitochondrial processing

3. α-Oxidation

Substrates: Branched-chain FAs (phytanate)

Unique Step: CO2 removal from α-carbon

4. ω-Oxidation

Substrates: MCFAs

Products: Dicarboxylic acids

activation.title: Fatty Acid Activation
activation.content:
Pre-Oxidation Steps

Acyl-CoA Synthetase

Reaction: FA + ATP + CoA → Acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi

Isozymes: Specific for SCFA, MCFA, LCFA, VLCFA

Energy Cost: 2 ATP equivalents

Transport Mechanisms

LCFAs: Require carnitine shuttle (CAT-I/II)

SCFA/MCFA: Diffuse freely into mitochondria

carnitine.title: Carnitine Shuttle
carnitine.content:
Mitochondrial Import System

1. CPT-I (Outer Membrane)

Action: Converts acyl-CoA → acyl-carnitine

Regulation: Inhibited by malonyl-CoA

2. Carnitine Translocase

Function: Exchanges acyl-carnitine (in) for carnitine (out)

3. CPT-II (Inner Membrane)

Action: Regenerates acyl-CoA in matrix

Clinical Note

CPT-II deficiency causes muscle weakness during fasting due to impaired FA oxidation.

beta_oxidation.title: β-Oxidation Cycle
beta_oxidation.content:
Four-Step Process

1. Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase

Reaction: Forms trans-Δ²-enoyl-CoA + FADH2

Isozymes: SCAD, MCAD, LCAD, VLCAD

2. Enoyl-CoA Hydratase

Reaction: Adds H₂O → L-β-hydroxyacyl-CoA

3. β-Hydroxyacyl-CoA DH

Reaction: Forms β-ketoacyl-CoA + NADH

4. Thiolase

Reaction: Cleaves acetyl-CoA + 2C-shorter acyl-CoA

Energy Yield (Palmitate)

7 cycles → 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 NADH + 7 FADH2

special_cases.title: Special Substrates
special_cases.content:
Non-Standard FA Oxidation

Odd-Chain FAs

End Product: Propionyl-CoA → Succinyl-CoA (B12-dependent)

Clinical: Methylmalonic acidemia in B12 deficiency

Unsaturated FAs

Auxiliary Enzymes: Δ³→Δ² isomerase, 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase

Example: Linoleate (18:2Δ9,12) requires 3 extra enzymes

Branched-Chain FAs

Pathway: α-Oxidation (phytanate → pristanate)

Defect: Refsum disease (phytanate accumulation)

regulation.title: Regulation
regulation.content:
Control Mechanisms

Key Points

CAT-I: Inhibited by malonyl-CoA (prevents FA oxidation when lipogenesis is active)

Dehydrogenases: Inhibited by high NADH/NAD+ ratio

Thiolase: Inhibited by high acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio

Fasting State

Glucagon → AMPK → ACC phosphorylation → malonyl-CoA ↓ → CAT-I activation

clinical.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical.content:
Metabolic Disorders

MCAD Deficiency

Presentation: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting

Diagnosis: Elevated C8-C10 acylcarnitines

Refsum Disease

Defect: α-Oxidation enzyme deficiency

Symptoms: Peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia

Riboflavin Deficiency

Impact: Impaired FAD-dependent dehydrogenases

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Why can't erythrocytes oxidize fatty acids?
They lack mitochondria - rely solely on glycolysis for ATP production.
How does ω-oxidation contribute to metabolic acidosis?
Dicarboxylic acids accumulate and can't be fully metabolized, lowering blood pH.
Why are ketone bodies produced during prolonged fasting?
Excess acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation exceeds TCA cycle capacity, leading to ketogenesis.
